title: The Song of Deborah (Judges 5:1–12)
hookLine: the war is sung again, and she calls herself "a mother in Israel"

lines: CHAPTER FOUR TOLD IT; CHAPTER FIVE SINGS IT.
cards: For a while, nobody used the main roads. Travelers took the back paths. Village life stopped.

That's how the song remembers the bad years, and it's a picture anyone who has lived through a frightening time might recognize: empty streets, people keeping out of sight, everyone going the long way round.
Chapter four told the war as a story. Chapter five tells it again, and this time it's sung. It opens: "Then sang Deborah and Barak the son of Abinoam on that day."

teach.h: PRAISE FOR THE PEOPLE WHO SHOWED UP.
teach.b: The song doesn't begin with the battle. It begins with the people who showed up: praise the Lord, when the people offered themselves willingly. It calls on kings and princes to listen: I will sing to the Lord.
And before any fighting, it remembers the God of Sinai, when the earth trembled and the mountains flowed.

teach.h: THE ROADS EMPTY, UNTIL I AROSE.
teach.b: Then it names the emptiness: the roads abandoned, the villages emptied, until, Deborah sings, "I Deborah arose, that I arose a mother in Israel."
A mother in Israel. Not a commander, not a queen, not even a judge, though she was one. She chooses a word from home.

Some readers hear in it a whole idea of leadership: care before command, someone who notices who's missing and gets people back on the roads. The song keeps widening the circle. It blesses the leaders who volunteered.
It calls to people who ride, people who sit in judgment, people who walk by the way.
It imagines the victory retold at the places where people draw water, the ordinary gathering spots, so the good news travels by word of mouth.
Then the song turns on itself: "Awake, awake, Deborah: awake, awake, utter a song." Even the singer has to be told to wake up and sing.
Rescue isn't finished, the song suggests, until someone remembers it out loud, together, and gives it a tune.

how: The Song of Deborah is read in synagogue as the haftarah on the Shabbat when the Song at the Sea, Exodus 15, is read from the Torah, known as Shabbat Shirah, the Sabbath of song.

games.q: a mother in israel — tap the pairs.

s: the song praises only the leaders
it blesses the people who offered themselves willingly, and the voices at the watering places.
Deborah calls herself a mother in Israel

before Deborah arose, the main roads were busy with travelers
the highways were unoccupied, and travelers walked through byways.

games.q: the battle is won and Sisera is dead. you're Deborah. what comes next?
o: a song, sung with Barak that same day.
back to the palm tree to hear cases.
games.why: then sang Deborah and Barak the son of Abinoam on that day. the story gets told twice: once as prose, once as a song.

practice: Bring to mind one thing that worked out lately, a hard day you got through, a recovery, a kindness that arrived on time, and the people who showed up for it.

Then give it a sound: hum a tune you know, or say it slowly with a little rhythm, the way the song turns news into music. No one needs to hear it but you; if you like, borrow the song's own words: awake, awake, utter a song.

wordCard.voice: Awake. The command the Song of Deborah gives itself, waking the singer up to tell the victory out loud. Today's word.
